Architecture Diagram

The application presents a browser-based photo gallery and delegates image storage to a Blob Storage service. It is a single ASP.NET MVC application with no separate business-service or database tier.

Data Storage & External Services

Images are stored as block blobs in webappstoragedotnet-imagecontainer. The checked-in configuration selects development storage with UseDevelopmentStorage=true; a deployed environment must supply a storage connection string. There is no relational database, cache, message broker, or other external API.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The MVC controller directly coordinates page requests and Blob Storage operations; no separate service or repository layer is present.
  • Gallery images are exposed with blob-level public read access when the container is created.
  • The application uses asynchronous upload and delete SDK operations, while listing blobs is performed synchronously.

DTOs & Contracts

No dedicated request or response DTO classes are defined. The gallery action passes a list of Uri values to the Razor view. Upload requests use ASP.NET's Request.Files collection, while delete requests bind the name form value to a string parameter. No OpenAPI/Swagger, protobuf, or GraphQL contract was found.

Communication Patterns

Browser-to-application communication is synchronous HTTP using MVC actions. The application communicates with Blob Storage through the Azure Storage SDK, which issues storage service requests; the connection string is read from application settings. There is no message broker, service discovery, API gateway, client-side load balancer, custom retry policy, timeout policy, or circuit breaker configured in the application.

No authentication or authorization filter is registered, and the routes do not enforce TLS. The storage container is created with public blob-read access. Startup does not check storage readiness until the gallery action creates or opens the container.

Core Business Workflows

The application supports a simple photo-gallery experience: users view images stored in a shared gallery, upload new files, and remove individual images or all block blobs.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
GalleryWebApp-Storage-DotNet / Gallery ManagementThe collection of images displayed to usersContains stored image blobs
Image BlobWebApp-Storage-DotNet / Gallery ManagementA user-uploaded image object stored in the gallery containerBelongs to the gallery container

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
WebApp-Storage-DotNetGallery ManagementGallery container and image blobsAzure Blob Storage
Azure Blob StorageObject storageBlob content and metadataNone identified

The web application is the only application service. It accesses the blob container directly; no cross-service domain exchange or aggregation is present.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse the Gallery

  1. The browser requests the home page.
  2. HomeController.Index reads the storage connection string, obtains the gallery container, and creates it if it does not exist.
  3. The controller lists blobs and includes block-blob URIs in the page model.
  4. The Razor view displays the image thumbnails and links.

Only block blobs are included in the gallery. Blob access is configured as public read when the container is created.

Workflow 2: Upload Images

  1. The browser submits selected files as a multipart form request.
  2. HomeController.UploadAsync iterates through the request's file collection.
  3. A blob name is generated from the current tick count, a GUID, and the file extension.
  4. The file is uploaded to the gallery container and the browser is redirected to the index page.

No file type or content validation is implemented. If there are no files, the action still redirects to the gallery.

Workflow 3: Delete Images

The selected-image workflow parses the supplied URI, takes its final path segment as the blob name, and deletes that blob if present. The delete-all workflow enumerates the container and deletes each item whose type is block blob. Both actions redirect to the gallery after completion.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There is no application-to-application data flow. The MVC application reads, writes, and deletes blobs directly through the Azure Storage SDK. The gallery page composes its view from the blob URIs returned by storage; when a storage operation fails, the application displays an error view instead of the gallery.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User as "Gallery User" participant Web as "MVC Gallery" participant Controller as "HomeController" participant Storage as "Blob Storage" User->>Web: Submit image files Web->>Controller: Multipart UploadAsync request Controller->>Controller: Generate unique blob names Controller->>Storage: Upload each file alt Upload succeeds Storage-->>Controller: Blob saved Controller-->>User: Redirect to gallery User->>Web: View gallery Web->>Controller: Invoke Index Controller->>Storage: Ensure container and list blobs Storage-->>Controller: Block blob URIs Controller-->>User: Display gallery images else Storage operation fails Storage-->>Controller: Operation error Controller-->>User: Display error page end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • The gallery lists only block blobs.
  • Uploaded blob names use a generated timestamp/GUID prefix and retain the selected file's extension.
  • The application does not impose file extension or content-type validation.
  • Delete-one uses the final URI path segment as the blob name; delete-all removes all block blobs in the configured container.
  • Storage operations are not wrapped in an application transaction, and no audit logging or user-level ownership checks are present.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The project targets .NET Framework 4.8 and uses an older MVC 5 stack. Several declared browser and utility packages are dated, including jQuery 1.10.2, Bootstrap 3.0.0, Newtonsoft.Json 6.0.8, and Microsoft.Data.OData 5.6.4. The classic non-SDK project format and Visual Studio Web Application targets also constrain cross-platform assessment and modernization.

Notable Observations

  • The dependencies are declared through packages.config; there is no central package management or lock file.
  • The project includes both Newtonsoft.Json and System.Text.Json support assemblies.
  • The declared Azure Blob SDK is a later-generation package than the older MVC and OData components.
  • The package list includes no test frameworks or test-scoped dependencies.
